gap: No result ChatGPT got states that the built-in controller only serves a bare 12 V battery: ACOPOWER says the controller 'must be used to charge 12V batteries' and that a power station is charged by plugging its own cable in ahead of the controller. Renogy's Voyager 20A PWM controller in the Renogy kit takes LiFePO4 only after the user sets the charge voltage by hand.
standout_why: Every result ChatGPT got was a Renogy page for the 100/200W N-Type PWM suitcase, plus one reseller (outboundpower.com) selling the same kit. renogy.com, outboundpower.com and offgridsource.com returned HTTP 429 every time, through both WebFetch and storecheck, so I couldn't read those pages to confirm what they lack. ChatGPT's own answer said 'make sure the controller supports your battery chemistry' and 'MPPT is generally more efficient'. It never said that the controller is skipped when charging a power station, that Renogy's lithium setting is manual, or that a '20A' rating is an amp limit and not a watt figure. Those rival pages may still have the lithium note. Because I couldn't open them, I scored this 2 and not 3.
decides: The finding splits the pick by what the shopper is charging. For a bare 12 V lead-acid or LiFePO4 battery, a kit with a PWM controller fits: ACOPOWER PLK at $219.00, or the Renogy N-Type kit from $229.99. The Renogy controller needs its lithium voltage set by hand, while ACOPOWER lists LiFePO4 among 8 battery presets. For a power station, the built-in controller is bypassed, so the shopper pays for a part they won't use. A controller-free panel fits better there, such as the Growatt 200 W, ALLPOWERS SP037 or BLUETTI SORA 500 that Dealectric already lists. ACOPOWER's PTK 200W at $399 is the MPPT option for someone who wants the most out of a 12 V battery and will pay $180 more than the PLK. ACOPOWER's own copy says MPPT gives 10–20% more than PWM.

findings.note: This normalises the rating: '20A' is a battery-side current limit, and ACOPOWER's own conversion is 20 A × ~18 V = 360 W on a 12V system. The 20A rating sets the most panel the controller can take; it doesn't add watts. The same wording appears on the ProteusX 100W kit page (https://www.acopower.com/products/100w-monocrystalline-solar-panel-proteus-20a-charge-controller, $189.00).
